knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"

library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("prehistoric_central_asian_steppe_and_oases.json5")

# Abstract

This paper reconstructs the demographic trajectory, macro-spatial distribution and settlement systems of prehistoric Central Asia from the termination of the Younger Dryas in 10000BC to the threshold of the nomadic Iron Age in 1000BC. Across eight biophysical catchments encompassing 3.890.946 km² (65.332 grid cells), aggregate population expanded from 40k (40.000) in 10000BC to 65k (65.000) in 8000BC, climbed to 220k (220.000) by 5000BC, and reached 520k (520.000) in 3000BC. The Middle and Late Bronze Age witnessed rapid socio-ecological divergence: intensive flood-recession and canal irrigation fostered dense proto-urban polities of the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC) across southern desert oases, while specialized equine and ovicaprid pastoralism expanded across the northern steppe corridor under the Sintashta and Andronovo horizons. Aggregate population climbed to 980k (980.000) in 2000BC, expanded to 1,15M (1.150.000) in 1500BC, and culminated at 1,45M (1.450.000) in 1000BC. Southern oasis valleys supported the overwhelming share of human numbers, led by the Zeravshan and Northern Bactrian valleys (304,5k), the Kopet Dag and Murgab oases (246,5k), and the Ferghana Valley and Middle Syr Darya (232k). This study calibrates territorial headcounts using Bayesian radiocarbon summed probability distributions, non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging across 442 domestic catchments, and 80 catalogued prehistoric settlements led by Gonur-Depe (8.000), Altyn-Depe (6.000), Namazga-Depe (4.500), Dzharkutan (4.000), Sarazm (3.500), Ulug-Depe (3.500), Togolok-21 (2.400), Dalverzin (1.800), Sapalli-Tepe (1.800), Chust (1.500) and Kent (1.200).

# Background

## Environmental Ecology and Post-Glacial Forager Horizons

The prehistoric human ecology of Central Asia was structured by sharp geographical contrasts between hyper-arid desert lowlands, well-watered piedmont fans and expansive continental grassland steppes [@Gill2025Ancient; @Allentoft2024Population]. Enclosed between the Caspian Sea in the west and the towering barrier ranges of the Tian Shan and Pamir-Alay in the east, the region relies hydrologically on glacial and snowpack melt discharged by major trans-regional rivers, notably the Amu Darya (Oxus), the Syr Darya (Jaxartes), the Zeravshan, the Tedjen and the Murgab [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Miller2026Cultivatin].

During the Last Glacial Maximum (c. 20000BC to 18000BC), hyper-continental cold and severe aridity restricted human occupation to sheltered piedmont refugia along the southern mountain fringes and riparian corridors [@Allentoft2024Population]. With post-glacial warming following the Younger Dryas around 9600BC, enhanced summer insolation elevated river discharge and stimulated the expansion of riparian gallery forests (*tugay*), shrub savannahs and productive perennial grasslands [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Gill2025Ancient].

Epipalaeolithic and Mesolithic hunter-gatherer bands exploited diverse seasonal ecotones [@Gill2025Ancient; @Conte2025Deconstruc]. In the Caspian littoral and Kopet Dag foothills, foragers occupied cave shelters such as Dam-Dam-Chashma and Jebel, hunting gazelle (*Gazella subgutturosa*), wild sheep (*Ovis orientalis*) and onager (*Equus hemionus*), while gathering wild pistachios and riverine molluscs [@Conte2025Deconstruc]. In the Pamir-Alay uplands, Hissar culture stations document mountain forager groups exploiting alpine ungulate populations with heavy flint macroliths [@Gill2025Ancient]. Across the northern open plains of Kazakhstan, mobile groups followed migratory herds of wild horse (*Equus ferus*) and steppe bison (*Bison priscus*), relying on microblade industries and seasonal riverbank encampments [@Outram2023Horse; @Zhang2025Genomic].

## Early Oasis Agriculture and the Jeitun Horizon in Southern Turkmenistan

The crucial transition to food production occurred along the narrow piedmont skirt of the Kopet Dag mountain range in southern Turkmenistan, where small perennial streams emerging from limestone gorges debouched onto fertile alluvial plains [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Miller2026Cultivatin]. Here, during the sixth millennium BC (c. 6000BC to 5000BC), the Jeitun culture established the earliest documented village farming communities in Central Asia [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Billings2022Agricultur].

At the type-site of Jeitun and related hamlets such as Chopan-Depe and Togolok-Depe, communities constructed small, single-room rectangular dwellings from hand-shaped clay bricks tempered with straw, featuring plastered floors coated with red ochre and domestic hearths [@Roberto2024Irrigating]. Archaeobotanical analyses confirm the cultivation of domesticated einkorn (*Triticum monococcum*), emmer wheat (*Triticum dicoccum*) and two-row hulled barley (*Hordeum distichon*), harvested with composite wooden sickles inset with geometric flint bladelets [@Miller2026Cultivatin; @Billings2022Agricultur]. Zooarchaeological assemblages indicate that domesticated sheep (*Ovis aries*) and goats (*Capra hircus*) provided meat, milk and hides, supplemented by opportunistic hunting of wild onagers and gazelles [@Scott2022Emergence]. Because annual precipitation across the Kopet Dag skirt averaged only 150 to 200 millimetres, Jeitun farmers developed simple flood-water diversion across natural alluvial fans, establishing the hydraulic precursor to Central Asian irrigated agriculture [@Roberto2024Irrigating].

Contemporaneously, the hyper-arid plains of the Kyzylkum desert and the expansive deltaic branches of the lower Amu Darya were inhabited by the Kelteminar culture (c. 5500BC to 3500BC) [@Conte2025Deconstruc]. Rather than adopting cereal cultivation, Kelteminar populations maintained an intensive foraging adaptation based on deltaic fishing, water-bird fowling and wetland mammal hunting [@Conte2025Deconstruc]. At sites such as Dzhanbas-Kala 4, Kelteminar communities constructed large communal wooden post-structures covering up to 300 square metres, roofed with reeds and boughs, with conical-based ceramic jars decorated with incised wavy lines and comb impressions [@Conte2025Deconstruc; @Dupuy2025Rocks].

## Chalcolithic Consolidation, Proto-Urban Metallurgy and the Sarazm Crossroad

During the fifth and fourth millennia BC, demographic growth and technical intensification transformed southern Central Asia into a complex Chalcolithic landscape [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @ENTEZARIAN2025Shahdad]. In southern Turkmenistan, the sequence is represented by the Namazga I to III phases (c. 4500BC to 3000BC), documented at major stratified mound sites including Anau, Kara-Depe, Namazga-Depe and the Geoksyur oasis [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto].

Village settlements grew substantially in spatial extent and architectural complexity. Communities constructed multi-room domestic compounds with adjoining courtyards, specialized pottery workshops and collective burial vaults [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto]. The invention of the slow potter wheel and two-chamber updraft kilns supported the mass manufacture of polychrome painted pottery adorned with geometric and stylized animal motifs [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @Dupuy2025Rocks]. In the Geoksyur oasis, eastward along the Tedjen delta, farmers excavated artificial canals several kilometres in length, irrigating large fields of hexaploid bread wheat and six-row naked barley [@Roberto2024Irrigating]. Copper metallurgy expanded to include cast axes, tanged daggers, pins and personal ornaments, sourced from polymetallic deposits in the Kopet Dag and Iranian plateau [@Berger2023Rise; @ENTEZARIAN2025Shahdad].

The eastward expansion of this Chalcolithic farming tradition established Sarazm in the upper Zeravshan valley of northwestern Tajikistan around 3500BC [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @ENTEZARIAN2025Shahdad]. Situated at the ecological junction between the high Zeravshan mountains and the fertile alluvial plains of Samarkand, Sarazm expanded into an expansive proto-urban centre covering over 35 hectares [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto]. Excavations have revealed monumental mudbrick residential architecture, circular storage granaries and sacred hearth sanctuaries [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @Anon2026]. Sarazm operated as a pivotal metallurgical crossroad: its workshops smelted copper, lead and silver extracted from nearby Pamir-Alay ore bodies, while its trade networks exchanged Badakhshan lapis lazuli, turquoise, chlorite vessels and marine shells connecting the Indus Valley, the Iranian plateau and the Eurasian steppe [@Berger2023Rise; @ENTEZARIAN2025Shahdad; @Desset2021Faced].

## The Eneolithic Steppe and Early Equine Management at Botai

In sharp contrast to the mudbrick hamlets of the southern oases, the northern and central Kazakh steppe witnessed the emergence of specialized equestrian adaptations during the fourth millennium BC [@Outram2023Horse; @Kysely2022Discoverie; @Grigoriev2023Horse]. The Botai culture (c. 3600BC to 3100BC), identified across the forest-steppe margins of the Tobol, Ishim and Chaglinka river drainages, represents a milestone in Eurasian pastoral history [@Outram2023Horse; @Gill2025Ancient].

At the type-site of Botai in northern Kazakhstan, excavators uncovered over 150 circular and semi-subterranean pit-houses sunken into the terrace soils, arranged in dense street-like clusters that sustained seasonal aggregations of several hundred people [@Outram2023Horse]. Faunal assemblages at Botai are extraordinary: more than 99% of several hundred thousand recovered animal bones belong to horse (*Equus ferus/caballus*) [@Outram2023Horse; @Kysely2022Discoverie]. Multiple independent lines of archaeological evidence demonstrate domestic equine management, including bit-wear damage on horse premolars indicative of bitting and bridling, lipid residues of mare milk identified on ceramic vessel sherds, and domestic corral enclosures delineated by high phosphorus and nitrogen soil concentrations [@Outram2023Horse; @Scott2022Emergence]. Equine transport and meat provisioning enabled human bands to exploit the vast open grasslands of northern Kazakhstan far beyond riparian corridors, fundamentally elevating the carrying capacity of the steppe [@Outram2023Horse; @Taylor2020Early].

## The Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex and Oxus Urbanism

The climax of prehistoric social complexity in Central Asia occurred between 2300BC and 1700BC with the fluorescence of the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC), also designated the Oxus Civilization [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Anon2026; @Rasulova2025Formation]. Emerging from the local Chalcolithic substratum of Namazga IV-V, the BMAC represented a network of fortified proto-urban oasis states distributed across the lower Murgab delta (Margiana) in Turkmenistan and the northern Bactrian valleys of the Surkhan Darya, Sherabad, Vakhsh and Kunduz rivers in Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Afghanistan [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Roberto2024Irrigating; @Bonora2021Seals].

BMAC settlements were characterised by monumental architectural planning [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto]. The premier urban capital of Margiana, Gonur-Depe, covered more than 55 hectares and incorporated an imposing central citadel protected by concentric mudbrick walls with rectangular projecting bastions, surrounded by a royal palace, administrative quarters, large ritual water basins and specialized monumental necropolises [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Anon2026; @Rasulova2025Formation]. At its peak around 2000BC, Gonur-Depe sustained an estimated population of 8.000 residents [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Roberto2024Irrigating]. Secondary centres across Margiana and northern Bactria exhibited similar fortified layouts: Altyn-Depe (6.000 peak residents), Namazga-Depe (4.500), Ulug-Depe (3.500), Togolok-21 (2.400), Dzharkutan (4.000, possessing a monumental fire temple) and Sapalli-Tepe (1.800) [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @GuarinoVignon2022Genetic; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto].

The economic foundation of Oxus urbanism rested on intensive multi-tier irrigation [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Billings2022Agricultur]. Engineered canals diverted deltaic channels to support diversified agricultural complexes encompassing naked wheat, club wheat, two-row and six-row barley, broomcorn millet (*Panicum miliaceum*), lentils, peas and flax [@Billings2022Agricultur; @MirMakhamad2026Seeds]. Intensive viticulture (*Vitis vinifera*) and fruit arboriculture flourished, while recent micro-botanical and textile analyses confirm early silkworm cultivation and sericulture pre-dating the historical Silk Road [@Zhou2026Silkworm; @Chen2022Morphotype]. BMAC artisans produced elaborate chlorite vessels, carved stone cylinder seals, composite female statuettes of chlorite and calcite, and sophisticated bronze alloy tools incorporating tin and arsenic [@Bonora2021Seals; @Vincenti2024Female; @Berger2023Rise]. Extensive diplomatic and trade networks connected BMAC cities with Harappan urban centres in the Indus Valley, Elamite and Proto-Elamite polities on the Iranian plateau, and pastoralist groups across the northern steppe [@Anani2024Findings; @ENTEZARIAN2025Shahdad; @Desset2021Faced].

## Steppe Pastoralist Horizons: Sintashta, Petrovka and Andronovo

While oasis urbanism peaked in the south, the northern steppe underwent an agrarian and technological revolution between 2100BC and 1000BC [@Grigoriev2025Indo; @Grigoriev2023Horse; @Allentoft2024Population]. Around 2100BC, the Sintashta culture emerged across the trans-Ural steppe and northern Kazakhstan, establishing heavily fortified settlements enclosed by circular or oval ramparts and deep perimeter ditches, such as Sintashta and Petrovka [@Grigoriev2025Indo; @Grigoriev2023Horse].

Sintashta communities integrated intensive copper metallurgy with pastoral animal husbandry [@Berger2023Rise; @Scott2022Emergence]. Crucially, Sintashta kurgans preserve the earliest documented light spoke-wheeled chariots in the world, accompanied by paired horse sacrifices, bronze cheek-pieces, and advanced cast weapons [@Grigoriev2023Horse; @Outram2023Horse]. Over the succeeding centuries, this technological complex expanded into the expansive Andronovo cultural-historical community (including the Alakul and Fedorovo stages, c. 1800BC to 1200BC), spanning thousands of kilometres from the Ural River to the upper Yenisei and the Tian Shan [@Grigoriev2025Indo; @Dupuy2025Rocks; @Ning2021Ancient].

Andronovo populations established semi-sedentary villages along river terraces, constructing large semi-subterranean timber-framed rectangular houses [@Dupuy2025Rocks]. Their subsistence combined intensive cattle, sheep and goat pastoralism with horseback riding, widespread dairy consumption and opportunistic flood-plain cultivation of barley and millet [@Scott2022Emergence; @Miller2026Cultivatin; @Taylor2020Early]. Large metallurgical centres, such as Kent in the Karaganda region (1.200 peak residents), exploited massive local copper and tin deposits to manufacture socketed axes, spear points and bracelets that circulated throughout Inner Asia [@Berger2023Rise].

## Mountain Corridor Interactions and the Late Bronze Agrarian Transition

The second millennium BC was characterised by increasing interaction between northern steppe pastoralists and southern oasis agriculturalists along the Inner Asian Mountain Corridor (IAMC) [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Chang2022Ancient; @Dupuy2025Rocks]. Transhumant pastoralist communities moving seasonally between lowland winter camps and alpine summer pastures mediated the exchange of crops, metallurgy and decorative ceramics across the foothills of Semirechye, the Tian Shan and the Pamir-Alay [@Chang2022Ancient; @Dupuy2025Rocks; @Taylor2020Early].

At foothill sites such as Begash and Tasbas in southeastern Kazakhstan and along the southern shore of Lake Issyk-Kul in Kyrgyzstan, archaeobotanical flotation has recovered broomcorn and foxtail millet alongside free-threshing wheat and naked barley dating to the late third and early second millennia BC, documenting the gradual integration of pastoral mobility with opportunistic cereal farming [@Chang2022Ancient; @Dupuy2025Rocks; @MirMakhamad2026Seeds]. Pastoral groups manufactured hybrid ceramics combining incised Andronovo geometric motifs with burnished oasis vessel forms [@Dupuy2025Rocks].

In the Ferghana Valley, this inter-regional synthesis culminated during the Late Bronze Age (c. 1500BC to 1000BC) in the Chust culture [@MirMakhamad2026Seeds; @REZAEI2024Bronze]. Settlements such as Chust (1.500 peak inhabitants) and Dalverzin (1.800 peak inhabitants) featured fortified citadels, densely packed mudbrick and pisé residential quarters, extensive storage pit batteries and stone sickle blades, supporting intensive irrigated farming alongside bronze metallurgical workshops [@MirMakhamad2026Seeds; @REZAEI2024Bronze]. The dissolution of the BMAC urban centres around 1500BC led not to demographic collapse, but to a structural redistribution of population toward smaller fortified agrarian hamlets (the Yaz I horizon) and mobile pastoralist confederations, laying the ecological foundation for the Iron Age Saka and Scythian polities [@REZAEI2024Bronze; @Zhao2026Tracing; @author2026Microevolu; @Saffa2025Reassessin].

# Methodology

## Territorial Partition and Ecological Catchments

To capture environmental diversity and cultural trajectories without spatial distortion, this study partitions Central Asia into eight biophysical catchments encompassing 3.890.946 km² across 65.332 grid cells (Table \ref{tab:validation-prehistoric}):

1. Southern Oasis Core (946.111 km²): Kopet Dag Foothills, Murgab and Tedjen Oases (388.334 km²), Zeravshan, Qashqadarya and Northern Bactrian Valleys (191.840 km²), and Ferghana Valley, Chach and Middle Syr Darya (365.937 km²).
2. Steppe and Desert Basins (2.479.605 km²): Northern and Central Kazakh Steppe, Tobol-Ishim-Irtysh (1.459.865 km²), Western Steppe, Ural-Emba and Mangyshlak Plateau (664.428 km²), and Lower Amu Darya Delta, Khwarazm and Aral Basin (355.312 km²).
3. Highland and Mountain Valleys (465.230 km²): Semirechye, Issyk-Kul and Inner Asian Mountain Corridor (377.744 km²), and Pamir-Alay and Upper Vakhsh Highlands (87.486 km²).

At each historical benchmark year $t \in \{-10000, -8000, -6000, -5000, -4000, -3000, -2000, -1500, -1000\}$, total catchment population $P_r(t)$ synthesises settled urban and village populations, rural agrarian hamlets, and mobile pastoralist bands:

$$P_r(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{K_r(t)} A_k(t) \cdot \delta_k(t) \cdot \omega_k(t) + H_r(t) \cdot \mu_r(t) + M_r(t)$$

where $A_k(t)$ is the documented spatial area of nucleated settlement $k$ in hectares, $\delta_k(t)$ is the residential density coefficient (calibrated between 120 and 200 persons per hectare for mudbrick oasis centres, and 30 to 60 persons per hectare for dispersed steppe settlements), $\omega_k(t)$ denotes the contemporaneity factor, $H_r(t)$ represents the number of domestic rural pit-dwellings or homesteads with mean household size $\mu_r(t) \approx 5,0$, and $M_r(t)$ accounts for mobile pastoralist groups operating in the hinterlands [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Roberto2024Irrigating; @Grigoriev2025Indo; @Outram2023Horse].

## Multi-Proxy Demographic Calibration and Habitation Multipliers

Demographic estimation across prehistoric Central Asia requires reconciling disparate classes of archaeological and bio-archaeological data [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Grigoriev2025Indo; @Allentoft2024Population]. For nucleated oasis centres, architectural floor area and domestic room counts provide robust baselines. Excavations at Gonur-Depe, Altyn-Depe and Dzharkutan demonstrate standardised domestic blocks of three to five rooms accommodating nuclear families of five to six individuals, yielding site densities of approximately 150 inhabitants per hectare [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Roberto2024Irrigating; @GuarinoVignon2022Genetic].

For steppe pastoralist communities, demographic scaling relies on kurgan necropolis dimensions, habitation mound areas and seasonal dispersion models [@Grigoriev2025Indo; @Scott2022Emergence]. In the Sintashta and Andronovo horizons, fortified settlements contain between 30 and 80 domestic longhouses, indicating nucleated village communities of 200 to 800 inhabitants surrounded by seasonal pastoral camps [@Grigoriev2025Indo; @Dupuy2025Rocks].

Chronometric calibration anchors these spatial baselines against Bayesian radiocarbon summed probability distributions (SPDs) compiled from regional databases, including CAAL dated horizons (5.073 entries), c14bazAAR/p3k14c syntheses (1.346 dates) and ancient genomic time-series corpora [@Allentoft2024Population; @Zhao2026Tracing]. Date frequencies are adjusted for calibration plateaus, marine and freshwater reservoir offsets in arid basins, and taphonomic destruction of mudbrick architecture [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Dupuy2025Rocks].

## Non-Stationary Kriging and Biophysical Covariates

Spatial population allocation across the eight catchments draws on the regional kriging domain, integrating 12.473 domestic assigned records across 442 domestic catchments (covering 65.332 valid grid cells, with 51.089 active land cells). Residual spatial dependence is modelled with Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging:

$$C(s_i, s_j) = \sigma_i \sigma_j \, |\Sigma_i|^{1/4} |\Sigma_j|^{1/4} \left|\frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2}\right|^{-1/2} \mathcal{M}_{3/2}\!\left(\sqrt{Q_{ij}}\right)$$

Regularised dimensionless variogram bandwidths stand at $\tau_1 = 1,5000$ and $\tau_2 = 2,7750$, with effective short ranges spanning 71,04 km across prehistoric horizons (Table \ref{tab:kriging-prehistoric}). The model incorporates five biophysical covariates: habitable land fraction ($\beta_{\text{hab}}$), natural vegetative productivity ($\beta_{\text{nat}}$), ecozone terrain suitability ($\beta_{\text{eco}}$), fluvial proximity decay ($\beta_{\text{fluvial}}$), and coastal or lacustrine buffer proximity ($\beta_{\text{coastal}}$). High-density settlement cores from 80 catalogued sites (led by Gonur-Depe, Altyn-Depe, Namazga-Depe and Dzharkutan) condition local density clusters, with urban masks applied to preserve rural population baselines [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning].

# Testing and Validation

Arithmetic reconciliation confirms exact parity between catchment population totals and aggregate regional sums harmonised from archaeological surveys and radiometric models. Table \ref{tab:validation-prehistoric} documents the longitudinal demographic trajectory across all nine benchmark years from 10000BC to 1000BC, decomposed into macro-regional groupings.

```{r tab-validation, results='asis'}
benchmarks <- c("-10000", "-8000", "-6000", "-5000", "-4000", "-3000", "-2000", "-1500", "-1000")

oasis_core_keys <- c("kopet_dag_murgab_oases", "zeravshan_surkhan_bactria", "ferghana_chach_middle_syr")
steppe_desert_keys <- c("northern_central_kazakh_steppe", "western_steppe_ural_mangyshlak", "lower_amu_darya_khwarazm")
highland_keys <- c("pamir_alay_vakhsh_highlands", "semirechye_tian_shan_corridor")

sum_group <- function(keys, yr) {
  sum(vapply(keys, function(k) as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[k]]$population[[yr]]), numeric(1)))
}

val_rows <- lapply(benchmarks, function(yr) {
  p_oas <- sum_group(oasis_core_keys, yr)
  p_stp <- sum_group(steppe_desert_keys, yr)
  p_hig <- sum_group(highland_keys, yr)
  p_tot <- p_oas + p_stp + p_hig
  yr_label <- paste0(abs(as.integer(yr)), "BC")
  data.frame(
    Benchmark = yr_label,
    Southern_Oasis_Core = viscount_fmt_pop(p_oas),
    Steppe_Desert_Basins = viscount_fmt_pop(p_stp),
    Highlands_Valleys = viscount_fmt_pop(p_hig),
    Total = viscount_fmt_pop(p_tot),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
val_df <- do.call(rbind, val_rows)
rownames(val_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  val_df,
  "Macro-regional demographic benchmarks across Central Asia, 10000BC to 1000BC, harmonised from archaeological surveys and radiocarbon models.",
  c("Year", "Southern Oasis Core", "Steppe and Desert Basins", "Highlands and Mountain Valleys", "Domain Total"),
  list(label = "tab:validation-prehistoric", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

Across all nine horizons in the regional kriging domain, Table \ref{tab:kriging-prehistoric} documents tightly constrained Matérn variogram parameters. Residual $R^2$ exceeds 0,999 across all horizons, with regularised nugget-to-sill ratios stabilizing at 0,04 across prehistoric and protohistoric epochs.

```{r tab-kriging, results='asis'}
sa_labels <- c(
  `01_epipalaeolithic_mesolithic_early_neolithic` = "1. Epipalaeolithic, Mesolithic and Early Neolithic (before 5000BC)",
  `02_chalcolithic_namazga_sarazm_botai` = "2. Chalcolithic, Namazga I-III, Sarazm and Botai (5000BC to 3000BC)",
  `03_bronze_age_bmac_sintashta_andronovo` = "3. Bronze Age, BMAC, Sintashta and Andronovo (3000BC to 1000BC)",
  `04_iron_age_saka_achaemenid_hellenistic` = "4. Iron Age, Saka-Scythian and Achaemenid (1000BC to 330BC)",
  `05_kushan_kangju_wusun_parthian_antiquity` = "5. Hellenistic, Kushan, Kangju and Antiquity (330BC to 500AD)",
  `06_sogdian_turkic_early_islamic` = "6. Sogdian, Turkic Khaganates and Early Islamic (500AD to 900AD)",
  `07_samanid_karakhanid_seljuk_khwarazmshah` = "7. Samanid, Karakhanid and Khwarazmshah (900AD to 1220AD)",
  `08_mongol_chagatai_timurid` = "8. Mongol, Chagatai and Timurid Eras (1220AD to 1500AD)",
  `09_uzbek_khanates_kazakh_zhuzes` = "9. Uzbek Khanates and Kazakh Zhuzes (1500AD to 1865AD)"
)
sa_horizons <- names(diag_data$variogram_models)
krig_df <- data.frame(
  Horizon = unname(sa_labels[sa_horizons]),
  Tau1 = vapply(sa_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$tau1_dimensionless, 2L), character(1)),
  Nugget = vapply(sa_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$c0_nugget, 6L), character(1)),
  Nugget_Sill = vapply(sa_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$nugget_to_sill_ratio, 2L), character(1)),
  Residual_R2 = vapply(sa_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$residual_r2, 4L), character(1)),
  Mean_Cell = vapply(sa_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]$mean_value, 4L), character(1)),
  P99_Cell = vapply(sa_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]$p99_value, 4L), character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(krig_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  krig_df,
  "Regional kriging variogram diagnostics across nine chronological horizons (65.332 valid cells, regularised tau1 = 1,50, tau2 = 2,78).",
  c("Kriging Horizon", "Tau1", "Nugget c0", "Nugget-to-Sill", "Residual R²", "Mean Cell", "P99 Cell"),
  list(label = "tab:kriging-prehistoric", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Table \ref{tab:source-corpora-prehistoric} details the component archaeological, radiocarbon and historical registries aggregated into the regional database, highlighting the contribution of comprehensive gazetteers such as UCL CAAL, Pleiades, Al-Thurayya and national heritage registries.

```{r tab-source-corpora, results='asis'}
src_labels <- c(
  ucl_caal_dated_horizons = "UCL Central Asian Archaeological Landscapes (CAAL) Dated Horizons",
  ucl_caal_typed_monuments = "UCL CAAL Typological Monument Gazetteer",
  althurayya_islamic_gazetteer = "Al-Thurayya Central Asian Historical Gazetteer",
  pleiades_antiquity = "Pleiades Ancient World Gazetteer (Central Asian Sector)",
  tegiszhol_c14 = "Tegiszhol Bronze Age Radiocarbon Corpus",
  c14bazaar_p3k14c_nerd = "Harmonised Global Radiocarbon Syntheses (c14bazAAR, p3k14c, NERD)",
  aadr_v66_central_asia_adna = "Allen Ancient DNA Resource Central Asian Compendium (v66)",
  archatlas_2020 = "ArchAtlas Central Asian Tell and Settlement Inventory",
  uzbekistan_cabinet_res846_register = "Uzbekistan Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 846 National Monument Register",
  kazakhstan_adilet_order88_register = "Kazakhstan Ministry of Culture Order No. 88 National Monument Register",
  published_excavations_atlas = "Harvard Dataverse Archaeological Atlas of Published Excavations",
  polaris_ia_ras_frontier = "Institute of Archaeology RAS Central Asian Steppe Excavations",
  jade_xinjiang_frontier = "East Asian Western Frontier Buffer Survey",
  central_asia_scholarly_catalogue = "Central Asian Prehistoric Settlement Scholarly Catalogue"
)

sc_keys <- names(geo_data$source_record_counts)
tot_sc <- sum(as.numeric(unlist(geo_data$source_record_counts)))

sc_rows <- lapply(sc_keys, function(sk) {
  lbl <- if (sk %in% names(src_labels)) unname(src_labels[[sk]]) else sk
  cnt <- as.numeric(geo_data$source_record_counts[[sk]])
  data.frame(
    Registry = lbl,
    Records = viscount_fmt_number(cnt, 0L),
    Share = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * cnt / tot_sc, 2L), "%"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sc_df <- do.call(rbind, sc_rows)
rownames(sc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sc_df,
  "Component archaeological, radiocarbon and heritage gazetteer registries aggregated into the Central Asian domain.",
  c("Source Registry", "Raw Records", "Share"),
  list(label = "tab:source-corpora-prehistoric", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

# Results

## Early Holocene Forager Colonisation (10000BC to 5000BC)

Between 10000BC and 5000BC, human populations across Central Asia expanded from low-density post-glacial hunter-gatherer bands into established regional foraging and incipient agricultural communities (Figure \ref{fig:traj-prehistoric}). In 10000BC, total domain population stood at 40k people (40.000), representing an overall territorial density of 0,01 persons per km² across 3.890.946 km² [@Gill2025Ancient; @Allentoft2024Population].

```{r fig-traj, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_prehistoric_central_asian_steppe_and_oases_trajectory.png",
  "Demographic trajectory of prehistoric Central Asia from 10000BC to 1000BC across regional catchments with historical uncertainty intervals.",
  "fig:traj-prehistoric"
)
```

Over the succeeding five millennia, ameliorating temperatures and expanding post-glacial vegetation supported gradual population growth (Table \ref{tab:regions-prehistoric}). Domain numbers rose to 65k in 8000BC and reached 145k by 6000BC [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Miller2026Cultivatin]. The pivotal transformation occurred along the Kopet Dag piedmont with the emergence of the Jeitun culture around 6000BC [@Roberto2024Irrigating]. Cultivation of domesticated einkorn and emmer wheat, combined with sheep and goat herding and small-scale stream diversion, lifted population in the Kopet Dag and Murgab catchment from 6,8k in 10000BC to 24,65k in 6000BC and 37,4k in 5000BC [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Billings2022Agricultur].

Concurrently, the fertile alluvial corridors of the Zeravshan and Northern Bactria expanded from 8,4k in 10000BC to 46,2k in 5000BC, while the Ferghana Valley and Middle Syr Darya grew from 6,4k to 35,2k [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto]. On the open northern steppe, mobile hunter-gatherers tracking wild equids and bison expanded the population of the Northern Kazakh Steppe from 6k in 10000BC to 33k in 5000BC [@Outram2023Horse; @Gill2025Ancient]. By 5000BC, domain population stood at 220k, with southern oasis valleys sustaining over 54% of all inhabitants (Table \ref{tab:validation-prehistoric}).

## Chalcolithic Consolidation and Oasis Expansion (5000BC to 3000BC)

The two millennia between 5000BC and 3000BC witnessed substantial socio-demographic consolidation across both oasis and steppe biomes (Figure \ref{fig:dens-prehistoric}) [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @Outram2023Horse]. Aggregate population expanded from 220k in 5000BC to 340k in 4000BC and reached 520k in 3000BC (Table \ref{tab:regions-prehistoric}).

```{r fig-dens, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig3_prehistoric_central_asian_steppe_and_oases_density.png",
  "Continuous kriged population density surface and territorial density comparison across eight Central Asian catchments.",
  "fig:dens-prehistoric"
)
```

In southern Turkmenistan, the Namazga I to III cultural phases introduced two-chamber pottery kilns, copper metallurgy, multi-room mudbrick architecture and extensive gravity-fed canal networks [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto]. The Kopet Dag and Murgab catchment climbed from 37,4k in 5000BC to 57,8k in 4000BC and 88,4k in 3000BC, anchored by substantial agricultural mounds at Anau, Namazga-Depe and the Geoksyur oasis [@Roberto2024Irrigating].

In the Zeravshan valley, the foundation and growth of Sarazm around 3500BC established a major metallurgical and trade hub [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @ENTEZARIAN2025Shahdad]. Population in the Zeravshan and Northern Bactrian catchment surged from 46,2k in 5000BC to 71,4k in 4000BC and 109,2k in 3000BC [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @Berger2023Rise]. Across the northern steppe, the emergence of the Botai culture around 3600BC drove horse management, bitting, milk exploitation and large nucleated semi-subterranean villages, raising Northern Kazakh Steppe population to 78k by 3000BC [@Outram2023Horse; @Scott2022Emergence].

```{r tab-regions, results='asis'}
yr_cols <- c("-10000", "-8000", "-6000", "-5000", "-4000", "-3000", "-2000", "-1500", "-1000")
yr_hdrs <- paste0(abs(as.integer(yr_cols)), "BC")

reg_rows <- lapply(names(mod_data$regions), function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) viscount_fmt_pop(rv$population[[y]]), character(1))
  nm <- gsub("&", "and", rv$name, fixed = TRUE)
  df_r <- data.frame(
    Region = nm,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(rv$area_km2, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
    df_r[[yr_hdrs[idx]]] <- vals[idx]
  }
  df_r
})
reg_df <- do.call(rbind, reg_rows)

tot_vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) {
  tot <- sum(vapply(mod_data$regions, function(r) as.numeric(r$population[[y]]), numeric(1)))
  viscount_fmt_pop(tot)
}, character(1))

tot_row <- data.frame(
  Region = "Domain Total",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(mod_data$total_area_km2, 0L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
  tot_row[[yr_hdrs[idx]]] <- tot_vals[idx]
}
reg_df <- rbind(reg_df, tot_row)
rownames(reg_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  reg_df,
  "Territorial population benchmarks across eight Central Asian catchments, 10000BC to 1000BC, calculated from regional JSON registers.",
  c("Territory", "Area (km²)", yr_hdrs),
  list(label = "tab:regions-prehistoric", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 20L)
)
```

## The Bronze Age Urban and Pastoral Climax (3000BC to 1500BC)

Between 3000BC and 1500BC, Central Asia underwent transformative demographic acceleration fueled by two distinct socio-ecological systems: intensive canal-irrigated urbanism in the southern oases and pastoral bronzeworking across the northern steppe [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Grigoriev2025Indo; @Roberto2024Irrigating]. Aggregate population nearly doubled between 3000BC and 2000BC, rising from 520k to 980k, and climbed further to 1,15M by 1500BC (Table \ref{tab:regions-prehistoric}).

```{r tab-density, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
dens_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  ar <- as.numeric(rv$area_km2)
  nm <- gsub("&", "and", rv$name, fixed = TRUE)
  n_sites <- sum(vapply(sett_data, function(s) identical(s$region_id, rk), logical(1)))
  p3000 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["-3000"]])
  p1000 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["-1000"]])
  data.frame(
    Territory = nm,
    Sites = viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L),
    P3000 = viscount_fmt_pop(p3000),
    Dens3000 = viscount_fmt_number(p3000 / ar, 2L),
    P1000 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1000),
    Dens1000 = viscount_fmt_number(p1000 / ar, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
dens_df <- do.call(rbind, dens_rows)
rownames(dens_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  dens_df,
  "Catalogued prehistoric settlements, 3000BC and 1000BC population benchmarks, and territorial densities (persons per km²).",
  c("Territory", "Catalogued Sites", "3000BC", "3000BC (km²)", "1000BC", "1000BC (km²)"),
  list(label = "tab:density-prehistoric", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 20L)
)
```

In the south, the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (c. 2300BC to 1700BC) established fortified proto-urban oasis polities [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Anon2026; @Rasulova2025Formation]. Gonur-Depe in the Murgab delta emerged as the premier urban centre of the domain, sustaining 8.000 inhabitants at its peak around 2000BC within a 55-hectare complex containing a fortified palace-citadel, fire and water temples, and specialized artisan quarters [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Roberto2024Irrigating]. Altyn-Depe supported 6.000 residents, Namazga-Depe held 4.500, Ulug-Depe housed 3.500, and Togolok-21 supported 2.400 [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @Billings2022Agricultur]. In northern Bactria, Dzharkutan expanded to 4.000 residents around 1700BC, while Sapalli-Tepe held 1.800 [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @GuarinoVignon2022Genetic]. The Kopet Dag and Murgab catchment reached 166,6k in 2000BC and 195,5k in 1500BC, while the Zeravshan and Bactrian valleys climbed to 205,8k and 241,5k respectively (Table \ref{tab:regions-prehistoric}).

In the north, the Sintashta and Andronovo horizons transformed the grassland biome [@Grigoriev2025Indo; @Grigoriev2023Horse; @Allentoft2024Population]. Spoke-wheeled chariotry, tin-bronze metallurgy and pastoral dairying enabled human groups to maintain dense permanent settlements along river terraces while deploying seasonal pastoral herds deep into the steppe [@Grigoriev2023Horse; @Scott2022Emergence; @Berger2023Rise]. Population across the Northern Kazakh Steppe rose to 147k in 2000BC and 172,5k in 1500BC, while the Western Steppe reached 68,6k and 80,5k (Table \ref{tab:regions-prehistoric}).

## Late Bronze Reorganisation and Early Iron Threshold (1500BC to 1000BC)

The second half of the second millennium BC witnessed structural realignments across Central Asia [@MirMakhamad2026Seeds; @REZAEI2024Bronze; @Zhao2026Tracing]. Climatic aridification and hydrological fluctuations in deltaic fans caused the gradual abandonment of large nucleated BMAC capitals such as Gonur-Depe and Namazga-Depe [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto]. Rather than demographic collapse, however, human numbers redistributed into smaller fortified agricultural hamlets and newly settled river valleys [@REZAEI2024Bronze; @MirMakhamad2026Seeds].

In the Ferghana Valley, the Chust culture developed an intensive agrarian landscape between 1500BC and 1000BC [@MirMakhamad2026Seeds; @REZAEI2024Bronze]. Fortified towns such as Chust (1.500 residents) and Dalverzin (1.800 residents) flourished, expanding the population of the Ferghana, Chach and Middle Syr Darya catchment from 184k in 1500BC to 232k in 1000BC [@MirMakhamad2026Seeds]. In southern Turkmenistan, the Yaz I ceramic horizon established fortified agrarian villages built upon high platforms, bridging the transition toward the historical oasis states of Parthia and Margiana [@REZAEI2024Bronze].

Concurrently, pastoralist communities along the Inner Asian Mountain Corridor (Semirechye and Tian Shan) integrated transhumant pastoralism with high-altitude cereal cultivation, lifting catchment population to 130,5k in 1000BC [@Chang2022Ancient; @Dupuy2025Rocks]. Across the northern steppe, late Andronovo and Begazy-Dandybai communities maintained large nucleated settlements such as Kent (1.200 peak residents), raising Northern Kazakh Steppe population to 217,5k [@Berger2023Rise; @Scott2022Emergence]. By 1000BC, domain population culminated at 1,45M people (1.450.000), with the Zeravshan and Bactrian valleys forming the demographic core with 304,5k inhabitants and a density of 1,59 persons per km² (Table \ref{tab:density-prehistoric}).

## Prehistoric Settlement Hierarchy and Urban Morphologies

The 80 prehistoric settlements catalogued in this study illustrate the structural dichotomy between southern mudbrick oasis centres and northern timber-framed pastoralist aggregations [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Roberto2024Irrigating; @Grigoriev2025Indo; @Outram2023Horse].

At the apex of the settlement hierarchy stood the monumental fortified capitals of the BMAC and Chalcolithic southern oases [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Roberto2024Irrigating; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto]:
1. Gonur-Depe: The premier urban capital of the Oxus Civilization, located in the lower Murgab delta of Turkmenistan, sustaining 8.000 inhabitants at its peak around 2000BC within an expansive complex of fortified palaces, fire and water temples, administrative quarters and royal necropolises [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Anon2026; @Roberto2024Irrigating].
2. Altyn-Depe: A major proto-urban centre in the Kopet Dag foothills, covering 26 hectares and supporting 6.000 residents around 2000BC, characterised by monumental stepped entrance complexes, elite priestly quarters and craft production precincts [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Roberto2024Irrigating].
3. Namazga-Depe: The stratified type-site of the southern Turkmen sequence, sustaining 4.500 residents around 2500BC across a 50-hectare mound complex [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @Roberto2024Irrigating].
4. Dzharkutan: A premier BMAC urban centre in the Surkhan Darya valley of southern Uzbekistan, housing 4.000 residents around 1700BC within a fortified citadel and an imposing monumental temple complex [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @GuarinoVignon2022Genetic].
5. Sarazm: An expansive Chalcolithic proto-urban metallurgical centre in the upper Zeravshan valley of Tajikistan, sustaining 3.500 inhabitants around 2800BC across 35 hectares [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @ENTEZARIAN2025Shahdad].
6. Ulug-Depe: A long-lived stratified settlement in the Kopet Dag foothill zone, supporting 3.500 residents around 2000BC with deep cultural layers extending from the Chalcolithic to the Iron Age [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto; @GuarinoVignon2022Genetic].

The second tier encompassed secondary BMAC centres, fortified Late Bronze towns and prominent steppe agglomerations:
7. Togolok-21: A fortified religious and administrative complex in Margiana, supporting 2.400 residents around 1600BC with concentric fortress walls and altar complexes [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Billings2022Agricultur].
8. Dalverzin: A prominent Late Bronze Chust culture centre in the Ferghana Valley, sustaining 1.800 residents around 1000BC within a fortified citadel [@MirMakhamad2026Seeds; @REZAEI2024Bronze].
9. Sapalli-Tepe: A planned square BMAC fortress settlement in the Surkhan Darya basin, housing 1.800 residents around 1800BC within multi-tier mudbrick defensive bastions [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @GuarinoVignon2022Genetic].
10. Chust: The eponymous type-site of the Chust culture in Ferghana, housing 1.500 residents around 1100BC [@MirMakhamad2026Seeds].
11. Geoksyur: A major Chalcolithic oasis settlement in the Tedjen delta, supporting 1.500 residents around 3200BC with complex irrigation networks [@Roberto2024Irrigating].
12. Anau: A stratified mound site near Ashgabat, housing 1.200 residents around 2500BC [@BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto].
13. Kent: The largest documented Late Bronze Age settlement of the Begazy-Dandybai culture in central Kazakhstan, sustaining 1.200 residents around 1100BC with specialized copper-smelting furnaces and stone architecture [@Berger2023Rise].
14. Botai: The pivotal Eneolithic equestrian aggregation site in northern Kazakhstan, supporting 950 residents around 3400BC across more than 150 pit-houses [@Outram2023Horse; @Kysely2022Discoverie].

## Analytical Limitations and Preservation Biases

Three taphonomic and methodological caveats condition precision in this prehistoric reconstruction. First, differential geomorphological visibility creates acute preservation asymmetries between riverine oases and open grasslands [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @Conte2025Deconstruc]. In the lower deltas of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, active river avulsion and shifting aeolian sands have buried early Holocene forager sites under metres of sediment, while mudbrick tells along piedmont fans are prominent topographic landmarks [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @BendezuSarmiento2024Protohisto].

Second, architectural contemporaneity introduces estimation uncertainty in multi-phase settlements [@Yoldoshev2026Osiyoning; @Outram2023Horse]. In large tells such as Gonur-Depe and Namazga-Depe, dense rebuild phases require careful stratigraphic Bayesian modelling to isolate concurrent domestic occupations from abandoned sectors, introducing an estimated uncertainty interval of $\pm 15\%$ to $\pm 25\%$ [@Roberto2024Irrigating; @GuarinoVignon2022Genetic].

Third, mobile pastoralist populations in the steppe and mountain corridors leave ephemeral architectural footprints [@Conte2025Deconstruc; @Taylor2020Early]. While kurgan cemeteries and seasonal camp scatters document substantial regional presence, translating mortuary counts into absolute living populations relies on demographic mortality models and ethnographic grazing capacities, warranting regularised kriging bandwidths to smooth local sampling variations [@Scott2022Emergence; @Taylor2020Early].
